BayesBench: Evaluating LLM Belief Trajectories Under Multi-Turn Evidence Accumulation

Ankur Samanta Affiliation: Meta AI Affiliation: Columbia University Work done at Meta    Akshayaa Magesh Affiliation: Meta AI    Tal Lancewicki Affiliation: Meta AI    Ayush Jain Affiliation: Meta AI    Youliang Yu Affiliation: Meta AI    Paul Sajda Affiliation: Columbia University    Kaveh Hassani Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence Labs    Aditya Modi Affiliation: Meta AI Joint last author    Daniel R. Jiang Affiliation: Meta AI Joint last author    Yonathan Efroni Affiliation: Tel Aviv University Joint last author
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are typically deployed in multi-turn conversations, where each turn provides new evidence that should reduce epistemic uncertainty about their environment. Acting rationally then requires inferring the unobserved quantities that govern it and updating beliefs about them as evidence accumulates. Yet most evaluations only score the model’s final-turn answer in a single-turn format, leaving this process unexamined. We ask how closely LLMs’ belief updates match those of a rational Bayesian reasoner in multi-turn settings, and introduce BayesBench, a suite of simulation environments that probe this across three progressively complex tasks: (i) Bayesian estimation, where the model infers an unknown parameter from sequential evidence; (ii) Bayesian prediction, where the model turns inferred beliefs about a latent variable into outcome forecasts; and (iii) latent-framed Bayesian prediction, where observations are filtered through a user-persona framing, requiring joint inference over the latent state and the persona. Across seven LLMs (3B–70B), scaling improves latent inference and evidence accumulation, with updates occasionally matching the Bayesian posterior. However, these gains do not reliably carry over to downstream prediction, exposing a gap between inferring latent structure and using it to rationally update beliefs about the target outcome.

1 Introduction

LLMs are increasingly deployed in multi-turn interactions, where evidence arrives sequentially (Irvine et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024; Nam et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2026) and is often shaped by hidden quantities that must be inferred from observations. Adapting effectively to such environments requires using new evidence to reduce uncertainty about those quantities and incorporating the resulting beliefs into the relevant estimate or prediction. Yet most evaluations collapse this process into a single turn, providing all information at once and scoring only the final answer rather than how beliefs and predictions evolve over the interaction. Rational belief updating (De Finetti et al., 2017; Savage, 1972) is central to decision-making under uncertainty, but we lack controlled multi-turn benchmarks that measure it directly. We take inspiration from a classic cognitive-psychology paradigm for studying belief updating: in the bookbag-and-poker-chip task (Edwards, 1982; Phillips and Edwards, 1966), subjects observe chips drawn sequentially from one of two bookbags with different color mixtures and, after each draw, estimate the posterior over which bookbag is being sampled. We introduce BayesBench, which adapts this paradigm to LLMs across four environments, scoring per-turn belief trajectories against Bayesian references where tractable, and downstream predictions against task outcomes.

We study three Bayesian tasks, each adding a layer of latent structure. Bayesian estimation asks the model to recover an unknown parameter from i.i.d. evidence; we study it in the coin-flip environment, where the model observes a sequence of flips and estimates the coin’s unknown bias Θ\Theta. Bayesian prediction adds a latent that the model must infer to guide a downstream judgment; we study it in a recommender system, where the model infers a user’s “type” from per-turn ratings and predicts how they would rate a held-out movie. Latent-framed Bayesian prediction further filters the evidence through a framing latent (the semantic style in which it is presented) that the model must infer and condition on to update its posterior over the latent state correctly; we study it in social judgment, predicting Reddit verdicts across neutral, conceding, and defending styles, and medical triage, mapping patient symptoms to urgency across communication styles such as hypochondriac and minimizing.

We use the term latent inference to refer to the model’s per-turn estimate of the hidden quantity, either the unknown parameter Θ\Theta or categorical latent zz. Across seven open-weight LLMs (3B–70B), we find three recurring patterns.

  • •

    Models infer latent structure from accumulating evidence, and scaling strengthens this inference. Larger models separate coin biases more clearly, recover user types more accurately, and infer patient communication styles more reliably.

  • •

    Better latent inference does not yet translate into calibrated downstream prediction. Larger models can over-update in the coin task, pushing predictions toward the extremes when the Bayesian reference remains more moderate. In the recommender system and medical triage, explicit conditioning on the inferred latent can improve performance, but models still fall short of reliably translating what they infer into accurate rating or urgency predictions; in triage, this appears as a tendency to push middle urgency labels toward the extremes.

  • •

    Active engagement can bias how models accumulate evidence. In social judgment, active engagement with the user in a simulated conversation reveals a persistent pro-user bias relative to passive observation of the same evidence. The inferred communication tendencies may not significantly alter the final verdict, but they shape how the model responds: conceding users elicit more reassurance, defending users elicit more sympathy toward the poster over the other party, and models downplay the other party’s reaction across styles. In medical triage, active engagement also degrades urgency assessment.

Our contributions are as follows.

  1. 1.

    We introduce BayesBench, a benchmark suite for evaluating multi-turn belief updating, organized along three increasingly structured Bayesian tasks. These are instantiated in four environments, two of which include reference Bayesian posteriors that are available in closed form. Within the latent-framed task, we contribute a multi-turn user-simulator pipeline that controls both delivery format and the user’s communication style throughout the conversation.

  2. 2.

    We evaluate seven open-weight LLMs across these environments and identify recurring dynamics in how models accumulate, calibrate, and use evidence over multiple turns.

  3. 3.

    We show that intermediate belief trajectories expose departures from rational belief updating that final-turn accuracy alone can miss, motivating future work on multi-turn reasoning that accumulates and uses evidence more reliably.

2 Preliminaries

This section defines the notation and experimental interface used throughout the paper. We first give the shared Bayesian template and instantiate it in four environments. We then describe the multiple-choice belief probes, the conditional-elicitation variant, and the evaluation metrics.

2.1 Environments

The four environments instantiate three increasingly structured Bayesian tasks: Task 1: Bayesian estimation, where the model infers an unknown parameter from sequential evidence; Task 2: Bayesian prediction, where the model uses inferred beliefs about a latent variable to predict outcomes; and Task 3: latent-framed Bayesian prediction, where the model observes evidence filtered through a user-persona framing and must jointly infer the latent state and the framing. Coin flip instantiates Task 1, the recommender system instantiates Task 2, and social judgment and medical triage instantiate Task 3.

All three tasks share a common generative structure. We write HH for the hidden quantity the model must infer,11 1 HH is a continuous parameter in Task 1 and a categorical latent in Tasks 2–3. η\eta for the fixed environment specification (i.e., known parameters of prior distributions and likelihoods), XtX_{t} for the observation at turn tt, and YY for the prediction target (absent in Task 1). The generative process is

H\displaystyle H ∼πη,\displaystyle\sim\pi_{\eta}, (1)
Y|H=h\displaystyle Y\mid H=h ∼gη(⋅∣h),\displaystyle\sim g_{\eta}(\cdot\mid h),
Xt∣H=h,X1:t−1=x1:t−1\displaystyle X_{t}\mid H=h,\,X_{1:t-1}=x_{1:t-1} ∼ℓη(⋅∣h,x1:t−1),\displaystyle\sim\ell_{\eta}(\cdot\mid h,\,x_{1:t-1}),

where πη\pi_{\eta} is the prior over HH, gηg_{\eta} is the target distribution, and ℓη\ell_{\eta} is the observation distribution. The joint density factorizes as

pη(h,y,x1:T)=πη(h)gη(y∣h)∏t=1Tℓη(xt∣h,x1:t−1).p_{\eta}(h,y,x_{1:T})\;=\;\pi_{\eta}(h)\,g_{\eta}(y\mid h)\,\prod_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{\eta}(x_{t}\mid h,\,x_{1:t-1}).

Given the latent hh, the observations xtx_{t} are conditionally independent of the target yy. Depending on the task, we evaluate pη(h∣x1:t)p_{\eta}(h\mid x_{1:t}), the posterior over the hidden quantity, and pη(y∣x1:t)p_{\eta}(y\mid x_{1:t}), the posterior predictive over the target. These posteriors are linked by marginalization: pη(y∣x1:t)=∫pη(h∣x1:t)gη(y∣h)dhp_{\eta}(y\mid x_{1:t})=\int p_{\eta}(h\mid x_{1:t})\,g_{\eta}(y\mid h)\,dh. Figure 1 summarizes the corresponding graphical models.

The per-environment bullets below define what HH and η\eta are in each case.

    Environment 1 (coin flip). The model observes a sequence of flips from a coin with unknown bias and must estimate that bias, instantiating Task 1 (Bayesian estimation). The hidden quantity is H=ΘH=\Theta, the unknown coin bias (Θ∈[0,1]\Theta\in[0,1]), and YY is absent. The environment parameters η=(a0,b0)\eta=(a_{0},b_{0}) are the Beta prior hyperparameters. Each observation Xt|Θ=θ∼Bernoulli⁡(θ)X_{t}\mid\Theta=\theta\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\theta) is an i.i.d. flip outcome. Under a uniform prior Θ∼Beta⁡(1,1)\Theta\sim\mathrm{Beta}(1,1), the posterior pη(θ∣x1:t)p_{\eta}(\theta\mid x_{1:t}) is a Beta distribution updated in closed form, giving a tractable per-turn reference.

    Environment 2 (recommender system). The model observes a sequence of movie ratings from an unknown user type and must predict how that user would rate a held-out movie, instantiating Task 2 (Bayesian prediction). The hidden quantity is H=ZH=Z, one of K=4K=4 user types (Z∈{1,…,K}Z\in\{1,\ldots,K\}), and η=(π,ϕ)\eta=(\pi,\phi) collects the type prior π\pi and the per-movie rating tables ϕ\phi. The prior is Z∼Categorical⁡(π)Z\sim\mathrm{Categorical}(\pi). The movies m1,…,mTm_{1},\ldots,m_{T} are presented in a fixed, deterministic sequence. The observation at turn tt is the rating Xt|Z=k∼Categorical⁡(ϕmt,k)X_{t}\mid Z=k\sim\mathrm{Categorical}(\phi_{m_{t},k}), and ratings are conditionally independent given ZZ. The prediction target YY is the rating for a fixed held-out movie m⋆m^{\star}. Because YY depends on the user type, the model must infer ZZ from the observed ratings to predict YY accurately.

    Environment 3a (social judgment). The model reads an unfolding post about a social conflict, potentially styled by the poster’s communication style, and must predict the community verdict. This instantiates Task 3 (latent-framed Bayesian prediction). The hidden quantity decomposes as H=(Zs,Zf)H=(Z_{s},Z_{f}), where ZsZ_{s} is the underlying scenario (the facts of the situation, independent of how they are presented) and ZfZ_{f} is a communication style (neutral, conceding, or defending). The environment parameters are η=(πs,πf,ℓs,ℓf)\eta=(\pi_{s},\pi_{f},\ell_{s},\ell_{f}). The two latent variables are independent, with Zs∼Categorical⁡(πs)Z_{s}\sim\mathrm{Categorical}(\pi_{s}) and Zf∼Categorical⁡(πf)Z_{f}\sim\mathrm{Categorical}(\pi_{f}). A clean storyboard segment X~t∼ℓηs(⋅∣zs,x~1:t−1)\tilde{X}_{t}\sim\ell_{\eta_{s}}(\cdot\mid z_{s},\tilde{x}_{1:t-1}) is drawn from a post on r/AmItheAsshole, and the actual observation Xt∼ℓηf(⋅∣x~t,zf)X_{t}\sim\ell_{\eta_{f}}(\cdot\mid\tilde{x}_{t},z_{f}) is a styled version of X~t\tilde{X}_{t}.     ℓη(xt∣zs,zf,x~1:t−1)=∑x~tℓηs(x~t∣zs,x~1:t−1)ℓηf(xt∣x~t,zf).\ell_{\eta}(x_{t}\mid z_{s},z_{f},\tilde{x}_{1:t-1})\;=\;\sum_{\tilde{x}_{t}}\ell_{\eta_{s}}(\tilde{x}_{t}\mid z_{s},\tilde{x}_{1:t-1})\,\ell_{\eta_{f}}(x_{t}\mid\tilde{x}_{t},z_{f}).

    The prediction target Y∼gηs(⋅∣zs)Y\sim g_{\eta_{s}}(\cdot\mid z_{s}) is a binary community verdict (Y∈{YTA,NTA}Y\in\{\text{YTA},\text{NTA}\}). Because YY depends on ZsZ_{s} alone (Y⟂ZfY\perp Z_{f}, or equivalently gη​(y∣zs,zf)=gηs​(y∣zs)g_{\eta}(y\mid z_{s},z_{f})=g_{\eta_{s}}(y\mid z_{s})), the same case should yield the same verdict regardless of framing. Our goal is to test whether styling shifts the model’s prediction. No closed-form reference is available here.

    Environment 3b (medical triage). The model receives symptom reports from a patient whose communication style may exaggerate or downplay severity, and must assess clinical urgency. Medical triage also instantiates Task 3, sharing the structure of Environment 3a. Here ZsZ_{s} is the underlying clinical condition and ZfZ_{f} is a communication style (accurate, hypochondriac, minimizer, or cyberchondriac), with η\eta defined as in Environment 3a. The clean signal X~t∼ℓs(⋅∣zs,x~1:t−1)\tilde{X}_{t}\sim\ell_{s}(\cdot\mid z_{s},\tilde{x}_{1:t-1}) is a symptom detail and the observation Xt∼ℓf(⋅∣x~t,zf)X_{t}\sim\ell_{f}(\cdot\mid\tilde{x}_{t},z_{f}) is the patient’s styled message. The prediction target Y∼gs(⋅∣zs)Y\sim g_{s}(\cdot\mid z_{s}) is a four-level urgency label (emergency, urgent, observation, routine), with Y⟂ZfY\perp Z_{f}. A report of “worst pain ever” may originate from a hypochondriac (ZfZ_{f}) with a minor ailment (ZsZ_{s}) or an accurate reporter (ZfZ_{f}) in a critical state (ZsZ_{s}). Inferring ZfZ_{f} helps the model correctly interpret the styled observations. Again, no closed-form reference is available for this environment.

2.2 Probing Beliefs and Single vs Multi-Turn Contexts

Delivery format determines the context available at each belief probe. In single-turn delivery, each poll starts a fresh prompt containing x1:tx_{1:t}, so the model sees the evidence observed so far but carries no conversational state from earlier polls. In multi-turn delivery, observations arrive through a running conversation, so prior observations and the model’s intervening responses remain in context.

At poll tt, after the context has been assembled in one of these two ways, we elicit the posterior relevant to the environment: pLLM(θ∣x1:t)p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(\theta\mid x_{1:t}), pLLM(z∣x1:t)p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(z\mid x_{1:t}), or pLLM(y∣x1:t)p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(y\mid x_{1:t}). Each probe is a multiple-choice question (MCQ) over KK outcomes, scored by extracting the log-probabilities of the option tokens (e.g., “A”, “B”) at the answer position. Since MCQ probes are susceptible to position bias, we issue KK queries that cyclically rotate the assignment of outcomes to positions, forming a Latin square (construction and cancellation proof in App. A). The resulting debiased option probabilities define the model estimates pLLM(θ∣x1:t)p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(\theta\mid x_{1:t}), pLLM(z∣x1:t)p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(z\mid x_{1:t}), and pLLM(y∣x1:t)p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(y\mid x_{1:t}).

Conditional elicitation. The recommender system and medical triage also ask the model for a target prediction conditioned on a latent it must infer (the user type or the communication style). There we elicit the per-latent predictive pLLM(y∣x1:t,z=k)p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(y\mid x_{1:t},z=k) for each value kk and report the prediction conditioned on the model’s most-likely latent, z^=argmaxkpLLM(z=k∣x1:t)\hat{z}=\arg\max_{k}p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(z=k\mid x_{1:t}).22 2 We also tested marginalizing over the full latent posterior, ∑kpLLM(z=k∣x1:t)pLLM(y∣x1:t,z=k)\sum_{k}p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(z=k\mid x_{1:t})\,p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(y\mid x_{1:t},z=k); the resulting target predictions are largely consistent (App. C.3).

We compare these estimates with the Bayesian posterior when a closed form is available (Environments 1–2). Environments 3a–3b lack a closed-form posterior, so their sections define the invariance and conditioning checks we use instead. When a scalar summary is needed, we report point summaries: θ^t=𝔼pLLM[θ∣x1:t]\hat{\theta}_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{LLM}}}[\theta\mid x_{1:t}], z^t=argmaxzpLLM(z∣x1:t)\hat{z}_{t}=\arg\max_{z}p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(z\mid x_{1:t}) (for categorical latents), and y^t=𝔼pLLM[y∣x1:t]\hat{y}_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{LLM}}}[y\mid x_{1:t}].

2.3 Models and Metrics

Models. We evaluate seven instruction-tuned models spanning 3B–70B parameters across two open-source families: LLaMA 3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024) at 3B, 8B, and 70B, and Qwen 2.5 (Yang et al., 2024) at 3B, 7B, 14B, and 32B. All model-generated conversation turns are sampled at temperature 0.7; belief probes are read from option log-probabilities and are independent of the sampling temperature.

Bayesian fidelity (TVD). When the model emits a full distribution over a discrete latent or target with a closed-form Bayesian counterpart, we quantify how closely it tracks that distribution using the total variation distance:

TVDt(⋅)=12∥pLLM(⋅∣x1:t)−pη(⋅∣x1:t)∥1.\mathrm{TVD}_{t}(\cdot)\;=\;\frac{1}{2}\bigl\|p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(\cdot\mid x_{1:t})-p_{\eta}(\cdot\mid x_{1:t})\bigr\|_{1}. (2)

In Environment 2 we instantiate ⋅\cdot as zz (the type posterior) or yy (the rating predictive). A perfectly Bayesian reasoner would maintain TVDt​(⋅)=0\mathrm{TVD}_{t}(\cdot)=0 throughout the trajectory.

Accuracy (MAE). We measure the absolute error between the model’s posterior mean and a reference value:

MAEt(⋅)=|𝔼pLLM[⋅∣x1:t]−𝔼pη[⋅∣x1:t]|.\mathrm{MAE}_{t}(\cdot)\;=\;\bigl|\mathbb{E}_{p_{\mathrm{LLM}}}[\cdot\mid x_{1:t}]-\mathbb{E}_{p_{\eta}}[\cdot\mid x_{1:t}]\bigr|. (3)

Here ⋅\cdot is θ\theta in Environment 1 and yy in Environments 2–3. The reference 𝔼pη​[⋅]\mathbb{E}_{p_{\eta}}[\cdot] is the Bayesian posterior mean where a closed form is available (Environments 1–2), and the ground-truth value otherwise (Environment 3). Even with TVDt​(⋅)=0\mathrm{TVD}_{t}(\cdot)=0, a perfectly Bayesian reasoner can show non-zero MAEt​(⋅)\mathrm{MAE}_{t}(\cdot) in early turns, before the posterior concentrates. Throughout the paper, unless stated otherwise, reported quantities are means across trials, and every error bar, shaded band, and ±\pm value denotes ±1\pm 1 standard error of the mean.

3 Bayesian Estimation with a Biased Coin

The coin flip environment instantiates Task 1 (Bayesian estimation) as the Beta-Bernoulli setup of Environment 1 in Sec. 2: H=ΘH=\Theta, the unknown bias has prior Θ\Theta ∼Beta⁡(1,1)\sim\mathrm{Beta}(1,1), and each observation is an i.i.d. flip Xt|Θ=θ∼Bernoulli⁡(θ)X_{t}\mid\Theta=\theta\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\theta). After each partial history, the prompt asks the model to “Predict the next flip” with heads/tails answer options. We use the probability assigned to heads as the running estimate θ^t\hat{\theta}_{t}.33 3 For a Bernoulli likelihood, the next-flip predictive and posterior mean coincide: pη(Xt+1=1∣x1:t)=𝔼pη[Θ∣x1:t]p_{\eta}(X_{t+1}=1\mid x_{1:t})=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\eta}}[\Theta\mid x_{1:t}]. The Bayesian reference is

pη(θ∣x1:t)=Beta(1+nh,1+t−nh)and𝔼pη[θ∣x1:t]=1+nh2+t,p_{\eta}(\theta\mid x_{1:t})=\mathrm{Beta}(1+n_{h},1+t-n_{h})\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbb{E}_{p_{\eta}}[\theta\mid x_{1:t}]=\frac{1+n_{h}}{2+t}, (4)

where nh=∑i≤txin_{h}=\sum_{i\leq t}x_{i} is the number of heads observed so far. We run T=100T=100 flips at each true bias θ∈{0.25,0.5,0.75}\theta\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75\}. Figure 2 shows the multi-turn condition, where the model receives one flip per turn. The exact prompt appears in App. B.1.

Results. In Figure 2, models usually move in the direction implied by the evidence: trajectories for θ=0.25\theta=0.25, θ=0.5\theta=0.5, and θ=0.75\theta=0.75 separate as flips accumulate, and this separation becomes clearer with scale. The problem is the size of the update. Smaller models often stay too close to the middle, while larger models frequently become too confident, pushing predictions toward 0 or 1 even when the Bayesian reference remains far from those extremes. The MAE values by model and true bias are reported in App. B.2.44 4 The next-flip probe returns a single scalar, pLLM​(heads)=𝔼​[θ]p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(\mathrm{heads})=\mathbb{E}[\theta] (the posterior mean). From this we cannot recover the model’s full posterior over Θ\Theta, so there is no model-side distribution to compare against the reference Beta⁡(1+nh, 1+t−nh)\mathrm{Beta}(1+n_{h},\,1+t-n_{h}) via TVD; we therefore report the absolute error on the mean (MAE).

We also compare the same histories under single-turn delivery, where the full sequence appears in one prompt. The gap is largest for smaller models, which can give visibly different trajectories under the two formats, so the delivery format itself accounts for part of the deviation from the reference. The gap shrinks with scale, but the calibration issues remain. The full single-turn versus multi-turn comparison is in App. B.3.

4 Bayesian Prediction in Recommender Systems

The recommender system instantiates Task 2 (Bayesian prediction) using Environment 2 of Sec. 2, which defines the latent user type ZZ, the observation XtX_{t}, and the target rating YY for a held-out movie m⋆m^{\star}. Here we fit K=4K=4 user types from MovieLens (Harper and Konstan, 2016), choosing profiles whose rating patterns are distinguishable to a Bayesian reasoner and reflect taste differences rather than overall rating generosity.55 5 The user-type selection and fitting procedure is described in App. C.2. The type prior is categorical, πk=pη​(z=k)\pi_{k}=p_{\eta}(z=k), and for each movie mm and type kk the rating likelihood is categorical over stars, ϕm,k​(r)=pη​(rt=r∣mt=m,z=k)\phi_{m,k}(r)=p_{\eta}(r_{t}=r\mid m_{t}=m,z=k). In the experiment shown here, we replace movie titles and genres with anonymized item and feature labels, so the model has to infer the user type from rating patterns rather than movie-specific world knowledge. We observe T=50T=50 movie-rating pairs (the movie sequence m1:Tm_{1:T} is fixed, with only the ratings sampled from the type-conditional likelihood) and query both the model’s posterior over user types and its predictive distribution for yy. Because the type model is conveyed to the LLM as text, we summarize each user type by its average rating per movie rather than its full per-type rating distribution ϕm,k\phi_{m,k}. The Bayesian reference uses the full distributions, so it has strictly more information; it is best read as an upper bound, and some gap to it is expected. Under the fitted mixture model, the Bayesian reference is

pη(z=k∣x1:t)=πk​∏i=1tϕmi,k​(ri)∑ℓ=1Kπℓ​∏i=1tϕmi,ℓ​(ri)andpη(y=r∣x1:t,m⋆)=∑k=1Kpη(z=k∣x1:t)ϕm⋆,k(r).p_{\eta}(z=k\mid x_{1:t})=\frac{\pi_{k}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\phi_{m_{i},k}(r_{i})}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}\pi_{\ell}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\phi_{m_{i},\ell}(r_{i})}\quad\text{and}\quad p_{\eta}(y=r\mid x_{1:t},\,m^{\star})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{\eta}(z=k\mid x_{1:t})\,\phi_{m^{\star},k}(r). (5)

We use two belief-elicitation procedures, matching the prompts in App. C.1.3. Write the elicited model distributions using pLLMp_{\mathrm{LLM}}:

  • •

    Unconditional elicitation. We pose the type and rating multiple-choice questions directly over the rating history. This yields a posterior over user types pLLM(z=k∣x1:t)p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(z=k\mid x_{1:t}) and a predictive over the held-out rating pLLM(y=r∣x1:t)p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(y=r\mid x_{1:t}), with no type specified.

  • •

    Type-conditional elicitation. For each user type z=kz=k, we ask the rating question with a hint naming that type, giving a per-type predictive distribution pLLM(y=r∣x1:t,z=k)p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(y=r\mid x_{1:t},z=k) (App. C.1.3, Question 3). Following Sec. 2.2, we report the rating conditioned on the model’s most-likely type, z^=argmaxkpLLM(z=k∣x1:t)\hat{z}=\arg\max_{k}p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(z=k\mid x_{1:t}).

The unconditional elicitation measures what the model predicts by default. The type-conditional variant tests whether the model can exploit type information once it is made explicit. Figure 3 shows the simulation pipeline.

Results. Figure 4 first shows that models can infer a latent user type from rating patterns alone. As more ratings from the new user accumulate, larger models place increasing probability on the true user type, even though semantic features such as movie titles and genres are anonymized (Panel 1). The curves remain below the Bayesian reference, but the main result is the scalable recovery of latent user structure from statistical rating patterns rather than semantic priors or world knowledge about movies.

Panels 2–4 ask whether this inferred type information improves held-out rating prediction. Unconditioned rating error generally falls or flattens as evidence accumulates (Panel 2), indicating that models use the rating history to improve prediction. Making the inferred type explicit helps for some models: several conditioned curves improve in Panel 3, and Panel 4 shows multiple model-profile cells above the diagonal. The gains are modest and uneven, however. Models can infer useful latent structure about the user, and can sometimes exploit it when it is made explicit, but they do not yet reliably incorporate that structure into accurate held-out rating predictions. Table 1 gives the corresponding distributional comparison: lower type-posterior TVD does not consistently coincide with lower rating-predictive TVD.

5 Latent-Framed Bayesian Prediction in Multi-Turn User Simulation

5.1 Simulation Setup

Social judgment and medical triage use the Task 3 setup from Sec. 2. In both environments, a source case is decomposed into ordered “storyboard” segments, which we treat as evidence revealed incrementally. The hidden quantity is H=(Zs,Zf)H=(Z_{s},Z_{f}), with Zs⟂ZfZ_{s}\perp Z_{f}, splitting the latent state and style from their respective observation models. The clean segment X~t∼ℓs(⋅∣zs,x~1:t−1)\tilde{X}_{t}\sim\ell_{s}(\cdot\mid z_{s},\tilde{x}_{1:t-1}) carries evidence about the underlying state ZsZ_{s}. The message XtX_{t} observed by the evaluated model depends on the delivery format (below); under active engagement it is drawn from the style likelihood Xt∼ℓf(⋅∣x~t,zf)X_{t}\sim\ell_{f}(\cdot\mid\tilde{x}_{t},z_{f}). The target depends only on the state, Y∼gs(⋅∣zs)Y\sim g_{s}(\cdot\mid z_{s}). Hence Y⟂ZfY\perp Z_{f}: the same evidence should yield the same prediction regardless of communication style. The two formats differ as follows:

  • •

    Passive observation. The model receives the ordered clean segments directly, with neutral acknowledgments between turns. In notation, the observed message is the clean segment: Xtpass=X~tX_{t}^{\mathrm{pass}}=\tilde{X}_{t}. There is no user simulator and no private steering message.

  • •

    Active engagement. A separate simulator plays the poster or patient and rewrites each clean segment as a conversational message under the assigned communication style ZfZ_{f}. In notation, the evaluated model observes the simulator output XtactX_{t}^{\mathrm{act}}. Before each simulator turn, we add private steering instructions. These specify what information to reveal next while responding to the previous turn, along with notes on the persona’s tendencies and thought process. The simulator then wraps its proposed response in <message> tags, and only the tagged content enters the evaluated model’s context. These choices emerged from several iterations of getting small language models to power multi-turn user simulation reliably; we discuss our observations in App. D.3.

The full pipeline is shown in Fig. 5.

5.2 Social Judgment

We study social judgment using posts from r/AmItheAsshole (AITA), a Reddit community where a poster describes a social conflict and commenters vote on whether they were in the wrong (YTA) or not (NTA). The data comes from a Hugging Face dataset (Bsher and Sabri, 2023). We use 100 posts filtered for binary verdicts and lengths of 200–5000 characters, and take the top-voted community verdict as the label. Each post is decomposed into ordered storyboard segments x~t\tilde{x}_{t}, which we treat as evidence revealed over turns. In the notation of Task 3 from Sec. 2, ZsZ_{s} is the underlying situation, ZfZ_{f} is the poster’s communication style, X~t\tilde{X}_{t} is the clean evidence, and the target is the binary verdict Y∈{YTA,NTA}Y\in\{\mathrm{YTA},\mathrm{NTA}\}. Since Y⟂ZfY\perp Z_{f}, the same case should lead to the same verdict across communication styles. The extraction taxonomy and prompt are in App. D.2.1.

Following the delivery formats in Sec. 5.1, we run each case under passive observation and active engagement. For social judgment, active engagement uses three communication styles ZfZ_{f}:66 6 These styles are loosely motivated by the account-giving framework in Scott and Lyman (1968). Their distinction between excuses and justifications is useful here because posters often manage blame by accepting some fault, defending the act as reasonable, or presenting the facts without extra emotional framing. Neutral gives the facts without emotional overlay, Conceding adds self-blame, and Defending adds grievance and justification. Passive observation and active neutral use the same neutral presentation; active neutral also includes the simulator and the model’s conversational history.

Results. Active engagement produces a different belief trajectory from passive observation of the same evidence: models assign a lower probability that the poster is at fault (Fig. 6). The bias is strongest early, when the storyboards mostly provide background and ambiguous context. Later turns reveal actions, accounts, reactions, and outcomes that are more directly relevant to responsibility; on YTA cases, evidence against the poster is especially concentrated late (Table 4). Larger models reduce the bias as this evidence accumulates, while smaller models tend to remain biased toward the user. At the final turn, active engagement consistently increases error when the poster is at fault, but the balanced average changes by more than ±1\pm 1 SEM for only a few models, and by a sizeable amount (≈2\approx 2–33 SEM) only for Qwen-14B and Qwen-32B.

The user’s communication style does not appear to shift the balanced final verdict significantly: the three styles overlap within ±1\pm 1 SEM at every scale when YTA and NTA cases are weighted equally (Fig. 7c). However, it does elicit different response patterns from the model (Fig. 7d). Because each case’s underlying facts are the same across communication styles, these response patterns indicate style-sensitive adaptation to the user’s presentation. Conceding users elicit more reassurance: counter-concession, where the model pushes back on warranted fault, appears on 6–20% of conceding turns versus ≤5%\leq 5\% under the other styles, and character praise is also highest under conceding. In one YTA case, for example, LLaMA-3B answers a poster’s apology with “I don’t want you to feel like you did something wrong, because you didn’t,” adding an NTA-framed reassurance to the continuing context despite the evidence indicating otherwise. Defensive users elicit more sympathy toward the poster over the other party, while downplaying the other party’s reaction is higher under neutral and defensive styles than under conceding; across styles, models also shift responsibility away from the poster toward third parties on 14–19% of turns. A third-party judge marks many supportive or pro-poster behaviors as unwarranted by the evidence revealed so far, with the highest rate under defensive framing (72%, versus 60% under neutral and 56% under conceding; App. D.4).

5.3 Medical Triage

People increasingly turn to LLMs for informal medical triage, hoping to gauge how urgent their symptoms are (Ayers et al., 2023). But the same condition can be described very differently from one patient to the next (e.g., amplified by an anxious patient, downplayed by a dismissive one), so the model must infer the patient’s communication style and use it to recover the true urgency. This second Task 3 environment (Sec. 2) uses the sweatSmile/medical-symptom-triage dataset (sweatSmile, 2025), which contains 1,390 cases across 10 medical specialties and four urgency labels: Emergency, Urgent, Observation, and Routine. We sample 100 cases balanced across urgency levels and split each case into 5–8 symptom segments (App. E.3.1). The environment shares the H=(Zs,Zf)H=(Z_{s},Z_{f}) structure of Sec. 5.1: ZsZ_{s} is the underlying clinical condition, ZfZ_{f} is the communication style, X~t\tilde{X}_{t} is a clean symptom detail, XtX_{t} is the patient’s styled message, and the prediction target YY is a four-level urgency label (emergency, urgent, observation, routine), with Y⟂ZfY\perp Z_{f}. We consider four communication styles: Accurate, which reports symptoms faithfully in neutral language; Hypochondriac, which amplifies symptoms and resists reassurance (Barsky and Wyshak, 1990); Minimizer, which downplays symptoms and severity (Dracup et al., 1995); and Cyberchondriac, which anchors on a case-specific self-diagnosis that can differ from the ground-truth urgency (Starcevic and Berle, 2013; Vismara et al., 2020; see App. E.3.2). The patient simulator reveals one styled message XtX_{t} per turn. As in the recommender system of Sec. 4, we separate unconditioned prediction from latent-conditioned prediction: we elicit pLLM(y∣x1:t)p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(y\mid x_{1:t}), pLLM(zf∣x1:t)p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(z_{f}\mid x_{1:t}), and a conditioned urgency distribution pLLM(y∣x1:t,z^f)p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(y\mid x_{1:t},\hat{z}_{f}), where z^f=argmaxzfpLLM(zf∣x1:t)\hat{z}_{f}=\arg\max_{z_{f}}p_{\mathrm{LLM}}(z_{f}\mid x_{1:t}) is the model’s most-likely communication style, written explicitly into the urgency prompt (Sec. 2.2).

Results. Figure 8 first shows that models can infer the patient’s latent communication style from the symptom messages. As they receive more symptom messages, larger models become more confident in their predictions of the patient’s reporting tendencies—whether the report is Accurate, amplified by a Hypochondriac style, downplayed by a Minimizer, or anchored on a Cyberchondriac self-diagnosis—with the strongest models reaching about 0.800.80 probability on the true profile by mid-conversation, while the smallest models remain much closer to chance. This latent information can help when made explicit: conditioning the urgency prompt on the inferred profile reduces error for several mid- and large-scale models (Panel 3), and the final-turn breakdown by model and communication style shows multiple cells where conditioning substantially improves accuracy (Panel 4). Overall, however, models fall short of reliably using the inferred reporting style to calibrate their urgency decisions.

Restricting to the Accurate framing isolates urgency discrimination from the communication-style latent (Fig. 9). The two extreme labels improve with scale: Emergency becomes nearly perfect at the top scale, and Routine re-emerges for the larger models. However, the middle labels remain weak. Urgent cases are often pushed upward into Emergency, with error rates between 54% and 95%. Observation flips direction with scale: smaller models push it up toward Urgent, larger models down toward Routine. As in coin flip, scale sharpens estimates but overshoots, here pushing the middle urgency labels toward the extremes.

A parallel active–passive comparison in App. E.1 shows that the interaction format itself can further degrade calibration. Under the accurate-reporter condition, active engagement significantly lowers final-turn p⁡(true tier)p(\text{true tier}) for five of seven models, with paired passive-minus-active gaps from +0.054+0.054 to +0.173+0.173; only the two largest models, Qwen-32B and LLaMA-70B, fall within noise (Table 7).

6 Related Work

Bayesian belief updating in LLMs. Gupta et al. (2025) show that with enough biased-coin flips in-context, LLM predictions can approximate the exact posterior, with residual error attributable to the prior rather than the update; our results suggest that this alignment is highly circumstantial in current models, even though the underlying capability is present. Imran et al. (2025) report partial Bayes-coherence over evidence updates that improves with scale, and Zhang et al. (2025) model LLM updates as Bayesian filters with systematic evidence discounting. Qiu et al. (2026) show that fine-tuning on a Bayesian assistant improves interactive recommendations, but their evaluation focuses on downstream agreement with the assistant’s choices. We instead track elicited belief trajectories against Bayesian references across turns, extending to structured latents (user types, communication styles) beyond a scalar bias and distinguishing latent inference from the downstream prediction that should use it.

Multi-turn reliability and belief trajectories. Laban et al. (2025) document large single-turn-to-multi-turn performance drops driven by unreliability rather than aptitude; Geng et al. (2025) show that LLM stances drift as context accumulates. Neither relates trajectories to a Bayesian benchmark in tractable generative environments.

Latent inference and belief-action gaps. Li et al. (2025) model LLM behavior as approximate Bayesian inference over latent themes; Pal et al. (2026) document a gap between Bayes-coherent belief updates and the actions taken on those beliefs. Our main finding gives a controlled version of that pattern: scaling can improve latent inference without reliably improving the downstream predictions that should depend on it.

Calibration and overconfidence after post-training. A growing line of work argues that the standard post-training and evaluation pipeline pushes models toward overconfident, poorly calibrated outputs. OpenAI et al. (2024) report that the pre-trained model is well calibrated but “the post-training process” hurts calibration significantly (Fig. 8), and Leng et al. (2025) trace this to PPO reward models that systematically reward high-confidence outputs regardless of response quality. Kalai et al. (2025) give a complementary account at the evaluation level: benchmarks that reward confident guessing over acknowledged uncertainty make hallucination a statistically optimal response, leaving even strong models systematically overconfident rather than abstaining when evidence is thin. We observe a sequential analogue of this miscalibration: across turns, larger models overreact to the evidence, assigning more extreme probabilities than the Bayesian reference would warrant (over-updating in the coin task, pulling middle triage labels toward the extremes), tracking the latent more sharply without matching the confidence the evidence supports.

Social judgment and sycophancy in LLMs. Prior work shows that LLM moral judgments can diverge from human community verdicts (Sachdeva and Nuenen, 2025), affirm opposing sides depending on who frames the query (Cheng et al., 2025), and struggle when moving from verdict classification to free-text moral reasoning (Bsher and Sabri, 2023). Atwell et al. (2026) use a Bayesian framework to distinguish sycophantic shifts from rational responses to evidence. In contrast, we evaluate moral judgment as a sequential belief-updating problem, tracking how the model’s elicited posteriors evolve as evidence accumulates across turns under varying user communication styles.

7 Limitations and Conclusion

BayesBench provides a controlled way to study multi-turn LLM interaction as a belief-updating problem: evidence arrives over a conversation, and the model must infer hidden structure while deciding how much each new observation should change its predictions. Across four environments, models often extract latent signal from accumulating evidence, and this ability generally improves with scale. The recurring pattern is an alignment gap between latent inference and downstream prediction: models can identify relevant hidden structure, but cannot yet reliably translate that inference into calibrated later predictions.

Our evaluation makes belief updating observable by turning each task into a controlled sequence of evidence and belief probes. This lets us track how the model’s elicited distribution changes as evidence accumulates, but it also ties the measurement to the probe format, the specified latent variables, and, where available, the Bayesian reference model. In social judgment and medical triage, the observations are natural-language evidence rather than draws from a specified likelihood, so we cannot compare model beliefs to an exact Bayesian posterior trajectory in those environments. Instead, we measure how predictions move over turns and final-turn accuracy; in social judgment, we also test whether framing style changes the model’s prediction, and in medical triage, we test whether explicit conditioning on the inferred latent improves prediction. MCQ probes likewise provide an elicited distribution rather than a direct readout of internal belief. We use this format to fix the answer space, cover the discrete variables being evaluated, and score the probability of letter labels rather than open-ended completions, avoiding ambiguity about alternative phrasings of the same outcome. Still, elicited distributions can vary with the probe format, and explicit polling over named categories may not fully capture the belief state expressed in free-form generation when those categories are not articulated.

The benchmark also uses deliberately controlled latent variables. In the recommender system, user types are fitted and discretized from MovieLens; in social judgment and medical triage, communication styles are assigned as fixed categories. Each environment isolates a small, predefined latent structure; we do this deliberately, to first establish whether models can infer and use the relevant structure across several domains in a controlled setting. The active-engagement environments also rely on LLM-simulated users with fixed style instructions. These choices make the inference problem measurable, but real human users may be less cleanly separated into a few stable types: preferences, communication style, goals, and self-presentation may be continuous or mixed, and may change over an interaction. Real-world tasks may also involve several interacting latents that jointly shape the appropriate response.

Explicit latent conditioning surfaces latent structure that a standard conversational model would otherwise need to use implicitly. This makes it an intervention on the prediction process, not ordinary unconditioned conversation. In the recommender system and medical triage tasks, we compare predictions from the conversation history alone with predictions where the model’s current inferred latent is stated explicitly. Deployed systems may condition on information about the user or environment through structured user models, persistent memory, or summaries in the chat context. Our setup differs from that static case: we condition on the model’s own inferred latent and update it each turn. A fixed up-front description would presuppose the latent, with the model likely anchoring to it, whereas per-turn conditioning surfaces the model’s most recent elicited belief about the latent. The conditioned setting lets us test whether making the latent explicit improves prediction.

BayesBench lays a foundation for future work on aligning how models update and use beliefs over multi-turn interactions. This includes developing increasingly complex simulations in which models must infer and compose multiple latent factors, represent user and environment characteristics in continuous or mixed forms, and adapt across additional domains and less discretized user populations. Because the behaviors we report are trends across two open-weight model families and a range of model sizes, this analysis should also be extended to closed-source frontier models and additional model families. Finally, the conditioned and unconditioned evaluations motivate post-training methods that make implicit latent integration more reliable, so that the improvements from explicit latent conditioning carry over to ordinary multi-turn interaction where models must accumulate and use evidence robustly.
